newsitem.title: UK: Platinum supply/demand balanced in 1997 - JM.
newsitem.headline: Platinum supply/demand balanced in 1997 - JM.

text.p: Platinum demand increased by only 40,000 ounces in 1996 to 4.88 million ounces and a similarly flat market is expected this year, according to Johnson Matthey's Platinum 1997 survey published on Monday.
"1997 will be a year of adjustment but we expect to see more demand in 1998," said Jeremy Coombes, general manager of marketing at Johnson Matthey's precious metals division.
The company is the world's leading refiner of platinum group metals.
The survey forecast a price range of $360-$400 per pounce for the metal against a fix on Monday of $388.75.

Supply of the metal fell by 90,000 ounces to 4.90 million ounces in 1996, reflecting an unofficial strike at the Rustenburg mine in South Africa and lower shipments from Russia, the second largest supplier after South Africa.

Industrial consumption rose by 95,000 ounces to 1.12 million ounces and jewellery offtake was up 40,000 ounces to 1.85 million, despite flat demand from the Japanese fabricators of 1.48 million ounces.

However, car makers cut platinum purchases for the second year in succession to 1.82 million ounces from 1.85 million in 1995 as the European and North American industries substituted cheaper palladium and as Japanese demand also declined.
But use increased among car makers in Latin America and South East Asia.

"Worldwide consumption of platinum in autocatalysts is forecast to fall slightly in 1997. We do not anticipate any substantial changes in platinum use in the USA but platinum's share of the European and Japanese gasoline sectors is likely to be further eroded," the survey said.
Lower demand in Japanese for platinum investment bars sliced investment demand by 105,000 ounces to 240,000 ounces.

Sales of platinum to China reached a record 200,000 ounces in 1996, up 54 percent on 1995 and reflecting increased demand for platinum jewellery and industrial uses like glass making and man-made fibres.
"Change occurred in smaller areas which we think will become more important in the future," said Coombes.
He said likely tighter emission controls in Europe by 2000 could mean more platinum being used. "The palladium market is tightening, which might help platinum to come back."
Russia was forecast to export less platinum this year than 1996's 1.220 million ounces, down 60,000 ounces.
"Platinum stocks have been contracting. Nobody knows by how much but there are probably not more than a year left in stock," Coombes said.
The survey forecast Russian shipments to be lower in future after stocks had been run down by an estimated two million ounces since 1990.

"Norilsk (Russia's main platinum group metal miner) will find it very difficult to increased production this year," said Keith Green, director of marketing for Johnson Matthey's precious metals division.

However platinum production is expected to rise this year from the two leading South African producers as Rustenburg recovers from a strike and Impala commissions its enhanced precious metals refinery.
South African mine output fell last year by 40,000 ounces to 3.33 million ounces.

"Profitability will be a key influence on future production in South Africa. Unless there is a sustained improvement in PGM prices, some companies may reduce output from higher cost shafts," the survey said. --Brian Spoors London Newsroom +44 171 542 8058
